Abstract:
Recursive self-improvement requires carrying accepted changes into later improvement cycles, while studying agent-proposed changes also requires substantial research infrastructure. Existing settings often leave agents to rebuild routine infrastructure or restrict exploration to individual components. We introduce RSIGym, an agent-native research environment based on Everything as a Service (EaaS). RSIGym exposes training, inference, rollout, evaluation, and sandbox execution through reusable services, with shared budget and permission controls supporting Data, Harness, and Joint improvement tracks. This design enables agents to investigate individual interventions and jointly optimize data, training settings, and execution harnesses within the same environment. We define RSI-Index as the mean fraction of the remaining performance gap closed across five benchmarks covering software engineering, terminal interaction, mathematics, scientific reasoning, and skill-based tasks. Comparing six frontier research models in independent Joint runs, Opus 5 achieves the highest RSI-Index of 0.4809 under a $500 platform-service budget per benchmark run. Its selected systems improve all five benchmarks, raising SWE-bench Verified from 17.67% to 50.33% and AIME from 31.67% to 97.78%. Additional experiments examine DSH-harness refinement, budget variation, and restricted network access, while recorded trajectories reveal how agents diagnose failures and select candidates. We open-source the full RSIGym codebase and results to support reproducibility and further research.

Abstract
From single-step revision to verifiable improvement loops
Recent advances in agentic systems allow AI systems to conduct experiments,
          interpret feedback, and modify their own workflows, transforming Recursive
          Self-Improvement from a theoretical concept into an engineering problem.
          Yet the field still lacks a unified account of what constitutes RSI and
          how its improvement loop should be evaluated.
This survey defines RSI boundaries, distinguishes four stages (evolution,
          self-evolution, meta-evolution, and recursive self-improvement) and anchors
          recursion in state inheritance: an accepted improvement
          from one cycle becomes the starting state of a later cycle, while
          “recursive progress” is reserved for the stronger claim that
          the inherited state also improves the improver. It introduces a common
          Proposal → Feedback → Optimization loop, organizes methods
          across four evolution targets, and identifies research gaps around
          evidence-based acceptance, reuse across cycles, and transfer beyond the
          tasks or evaluators that produced the gains.
Definition
A common loop for modern RSI systems
RSI is anchored in state inheritance: an improvement accepted in one
              cycle is retained as the starting state of a later cycle. Recursive
              progress (the stronger claim that the inherited state also
              improves the improver) is treated separately.
Proposal
Select an editable target and generate a candidate change through
                  prompting, search, evolution, program synthesis, training, or experimentation.
Target selection identifies what the loop is allowed to change.
Candidate generation creates concrete artifacts such as prompts, tools, memory, code, data, or checkpoints.
Feedback
Expose consequences in a repository, simulator, benchmark, training run,
                  or live environment, then convert outcomes into evidence.
Execution environments reveal behavioral effects of a candidate.
Verification signals judge the evidence through tests, rewards, model judges, formal checks, or review.
Optimization
Retain, revise, reject, promote, or roll back the candidate while preserving
                  memory, provenance, versioning, and validation evidence.
Update policies decide whether an apparent gain should persist.
Memory and lineage determine whether later cycles can reuse or audit the change.
System Structure
What changes, how it is tested, and what persists
Across the systems we survey, the same anatomy recurs: a target is
            edited, the edit is exposed to an environment that produces evidence,
            and a decision layer retains or discards it. Six components organize
            these concerns into three stages: what can be modified, how it is
            tested, and what persists.
Proposal
Choose what to change, then generate a candidate through prompting, search, evolution, synthesis, or training.
Feedback
Run the change and turn its consequences into evidence via reference, rubric, and judge.
Optimization
Decide what persists and what is saved, tracked, and reused across cycles.
Taxonomy
Four targets of RSI-related evolution
The four targets form a progression by persistence: behavior-level
            gains last for a single trajectory, agent-level changes outlive the
            current run, model-and-data changes transfer across tasks, and
            research-process evolution aims to improve the loop that produces
            improvements itself.
Behavior Evolution
Output self-refine, test-time evolution, and state optimization improve
                behavior around the current task or trajectory.
Output self-refine
Test-time evolution
State optimization
Agent-System Evolution
Workflow, memory, code rewriting, and harness evolution change the machinery
                that produces future agent behavior.
Workflow evolution
Memory evolution
Code rewriting and harness evolution
Model and Data Evolution
Synthetic data, meta-rewarding, post-training, and self-play alter the
                learning signal or model parameters themselves.
Synthetic data
Meta-rewarding and post-training
Self-play evolution
Research-Process Evolution
Scientific operation agents, AI4AI, MLE, and end-to-end AI scientist systems
                automate the research loop around AI improvement.
Scientific operation agents
AI4AI and MLE
End-to-end AI scientist systems
An evidence ladder: from local repair to compounding
Self-improvement claims differ in strength, and the ladder orders
            them by the evidence each one needs.
Local repair
fixes the current output and stops there;
persistent
            transfer
makes a change outlive the current run and help
            later instances;
recursive inheritance
(the
            minimal RSI claim) makes an accepted improvement the starting
            state of a later cycle; and
recursive progress
further shows that the inherited state improves the improver itself.
Causal attribution
supplies the supporting evidence
            (a counterfactual control against a frozen or no-retention
            baseline) that a retained intervention, not an unrelated
            confound, produced the gain;
compounding
is the
            claim that recursive-progress gains repeat across cycles.
Future Directions
An evidence-oriented evaluation profile
The seven properties below form a single evidence-oriented evaluation
              profile rather than seven independent capabilities. The organizing test
              is acceptance, reuse, and transfer: an accepted change must be credible,
              usable in later cycles, and helpful beyond the evaluator that admitted it.
Reliability
Does the change improve the intended capability, not just the measured score?
False positives can be written into memory, skills, or release pipelines; evaluations should report exploit resistance, calibration, trajectory integrity, and held-out transfer.
Efficiency
Can the loop improve within finite compute, time, and review budgets?
RSI needs cost frontiers: gains should be measured against compute, wall-clock time, failed attempts, deployment cost, and review burden.
Diversity
Do proposals cover meaningfully different hypotheses and execution paths?
Diversity is about causal independence, not just different wording; systems should preserve disagreement, branch distance, and failure coverage.
Persistence
Does a successful intervention remain available and useful later?
Retained artifacts need provenance, scope conditions, retirement criteria, and evidence that they contribute downstream rather than drifting into noise.
Adaptability
Can the system respond to changing tasks, tools, evaluators, and environments?
The key split is frozen evidence for comparison versus adaptive evidence for discovering new weaknesses as the environment changes.
Controllability
Are authority, review, monitoring, and rollback coupled to risk?
Update authority should track target scope, verifier strength, deployment context, and failure severity, with intervention points preserved across the loop.
Generalization
Does the improvement transfer beyond its original task and evaluator?
The strongest claim is transfer of the improvement procedure itself: later generations should search, evaluate, or optimize better because of what was retained.
Recursive self-improvement has moved from theory to engineering practice;
          the remaining challenge is to make its gains credible, reusable, and
          transferable beyond the tasks and evaluators that produced them.

Abstract:
AI systems increasingly participate in their own improvement: revising their outputs, adapting their harnesses during deployment, training on data they generate, and conducting AI research itself. This literature uses a vocabulary ("self-refine," "self-reward," "self-play," "self-evolve") that conflates fundamentally different ambitions. We survey 1,250 arXiv papers (2024-2026) along two axes: what the system improves -- its behavior in deployment, its policy through training, its evaluator, or the research process itself -- and the degree of loop closure (human-in-the-loop to fully closed). The taxonomy separates bounded self-refinement -- convergent, evaluable, and industrial practice -- from open-ended recursive self-improvement (RSI), which remains bounded by grounding requirements, collapse dynamics, and compute constraints on every measured axis. Its distinctive feature is a dedicated category for self-evaluation: every improvement loop is a claim that some signal can substitute for human judgment. We survey the evaluator design space -- judges, process reward models, verifiers, rubrics, meta-evaluation -- order the signals into a verification hierarchy from formal verifiers (strongest) to intrinsic self-assessment (weakest), and observe that demonstrated self-improvement strength tracks this hierarchy, that its failure modes (self-confirming loops, model and diversity collapse) follow from its violations, and that the "research direction-setting" bottleneck keeping humans in the loop divides into a verification problem the hierarchy indexes and a prior one -- choosing what deserves evaluation at all -- that it does not. We connect the literature to the theory of RSI limits and to the safety and governance questions raised by frontier-lab accounts of closing the loop, and identify governance-grade measurement of self-improvement as the field's most underpopulated niche.

# Research report

RSI-Index（RSIGym，Recursive Self-Improvement，递归自我改进）有哪些现存的相关工作？请区分 RSI-Index 本身与递归自我改进领域的相关研究，列出论文或项目名称、主要贡献和来源链接。

## Answer

现有证据中，RSI-Index 是 RSIGym 论文（arXiv:2610.10310）定义的评估指标，而非一个独立项目；RSIGym 是配套的 agent-native 研究环境。递归自我改进领域的相关工作在证据中包括三篇综述：Awesome-RSI-Research 的《Towards AI That Improves Itself: A Survey of Recursive Self-Improvement》、arXiv:2607.07663《Recursive Self-Improvement in AI: From Bounded Self-Refinement to Autonomous Research Loops》和 arXiv:2610.35193《Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models》。证据未提供 STOP、Gödel Agent、Darwin Gödel Machine、AlphaEvolve、SEAL、Self-Rewarding 等具体系统的名称、贡献或链接。 [E1] [E3] [E6] [E7] [E12] [E13] [E18] [E19]

## Supported findings

- RSI-Index 是 RSIGym 论文（arXiv:2610.10310）中定义的指标：五个基准上剩余性能差距被弥合的平均比例；RSIGym 是基于 Everything as a Service 的 agent-native 研究环境，支持 Data、Harness、Joint 改进轨道。 [E1] [E3]
- RSIGym 论文报告 Opus 5 在独立 Joint 运行中取得最高 RSI-Index 0.4809（每基准运行 500 美元平台服务预算），并将 SWE-bench Verified 从 17.67% 提升到 50.33%、AIME 从 31.67% 提升到 97.78%。 [E1]
- Awesome-RSI-Research 的综述《Towards AI That Improves Itself: A Survey of Recursive Self-Improvement》（作者 Hanjing Li、Qiguang Chen 等）界定 RSI 边界，区分 evolution、self-evolution、meta-evolution、recursive self-improvement 四阶段，以状态继承锚定递归，并提出 Proposal → Feedback → Optimization 循环。来源：https://lee1003-lee.github.io/Awesome-RSI-Research/ [E6] [E7]
- arXiv:2607.07663《Recursive Self-Improvement in AI: From Bounded Self-Refinement to Autonomous Research Loops》（Mingguang Chen、Licheng Wang、Bo Qu）调查 1,250 篇 2024–2026 年 arXiv 论文，沿“改进对象”和“闭环程度”两轴分类，区分有界自我精炼与开放式 RSI，并建立从形式验证器到内在自评的验证层级。来源：https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07663 [E12] [E13]
- arXiv:2610.35193《Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement in the Era of Large Models: Foundation, Risks, Evaluation and Open Challenges》（Jiayue Pu 等）提出 RSI 的操作性定义与流程框架，将可信 RSI 要求组织为真实持续改进、行为约束/对齐/公平、系统安全与隐私、透明与可控四个主题。来源：https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35193 [E18] [E19]
- 区分方式：RSI-Index 是 RSIGym 论文提出的量化评估指标（衡量跨五个基准的差距弥合比例），RSIGym 是其配套环境；而上述综述属于对 RSI 领域方法、分类与可信性要求的整体梳理，并非 RSI-Index 本身。 [E1] [E3] [E7] [E12] [E19]

## Unresolved questions

- 证据中未出现 STOP、Gödel Agent、Darwin Gödel Machine、AlphaEvolve、SEAL、Self-Rewarding 等具体 RSI 系统的名称、主要贡献或来源链接，因此无法列出这些条目。
- 未检索到除 RSIGym 论文外其他使用或定义 RSI-Index 的工作。
